query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (≈1 at.%) of aluminum to the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy will promote the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high‐temperature exposure in air, thereby significantly enhancing its oxygen resistance while maintaining its intrinsic room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with demonstrated ductility (8–16% at RT) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) but inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Microalloying by adding ~1 at.% Al during alloy preparation.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical testing at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C) under comparable strain rate conditions (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective, slow-growing, continuous Al2O3 scale at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen and, when present in minor amounts, oxidizes preferentially to form a dense and adherent Al2O3 film. This scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the substrate, mitigating pesting and preserving the bulk microstructure that governs the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy will show significantly reduced oxidation (evidenced by lower weight gain and minimal oxide scale spallation) after 5 hours at 800 °C, while its room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength remain comparable to those of the untreated equiatomic alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy under the same high-temperature oxidative conditions, which demonstrates extensive oxidation leading to performance degradation.
generation.boundary: Intervention is expected to be effective for high-temperature exposure in air up to about 800 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours; results outside this temperature/time window or with higher Al contents might lead to undesirable phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum Al content and the long-term stability of the Al2O3 scale under cyclic or prolonged service conditions remain to be established. There is also uncertainty about potential subtle changes in bulk microstructure if the Al content is not carefully controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one set with the standard equiatomic composition and another set doped with ~1 at.% Al. Subject both sets to identical oxidation tests by exposing them in air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Afterwards, characterize the surface and cross-sectional oxide scales using microscopy (SEM/TEM) and measure weight gain. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) to evaluate any changes in ductility and strength.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and continuity (via SEM/TEM)
XRD phase analysis of surface and bulk
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar weight gain and oxide scale spallation as the undoped alloy) or if its room-temperature ductility and 1000 °C yield strength degrade relative to the untreated equiatomic alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution.
